name: John J. Glessner House

present_status.note: Verified 2026-09-30 on the museum's official history page. The 1946 endpoint belongs to this modeled exterior phase: conversion for the Lithographic Technical Foundation changed the building, not ended its existence. This present-day status does not extend the unchanged 1904 model through the present.

documented_range.note: FROM: the family moved in in December 1887 (Glessner 1923; HABS data p. 1), and the February 1888 Inland Architect photograph shows the finished exterior; the day of the month is not stated, so the range opens on the 1st. TO: the research-centre conversion of September 1946 (HABS data p. 2) — stable door replaced, loft door closed up, courtyard paved — is the first exterior change recorded. The 1892 changes were interior. The phase is modelled as it stood on 1 July 1904, the scene date; values carried from the 1963-65 survey are ones the 1888 photograph brackets or the 1946 list does not touch (docs/RESEARCH/glessner_house_1904.md § 2).

position.symbolic_location: 1800 S. Prairie Avenue: the south-west corner of Prairie Avenue and E. 18th Street, on parcel prairie_1800 (data/street_grid/1904.json).
position.note: ON THE T-0474 PARCEL. data/street_grid/1904.json parcel prairie_1800 (Sanborn 1911 sheet 28) puts the lot's NE street corner at local E 1392.05, N -3217.24 and its NW rear corner at E 1338.07, N -3217.87. The house's north face stands on that 18th Street line and its east face 14.7 ft (4.481 m) behind the Prairie Avenue line — T-1731's reading of the same sheet at 6.0 px/ft, +/- 1.5 ft. Its NE corner is therefore E 1387.570, N -3217.292, and the footprint's origin (the SW corner of its bounding box) E 1338.687, N -3240.420. Rotation -0.669 degrees is the 18th Street line's own bearing (89.331 degrees, west to east) less 90, the long face's alignment. RECONCILED WITH THE PARCEL: the parcel is 177.1 ft deep, the house 161.25 ft plus the 14.7 ft setback, so the west face stands 0.35 m (1.16 ft) inside the parcel's alley line rather than on it; both readings carry more tolerance than that (+/- 1.5 ft on the setback, the parcel's own lines inferred), and the setback is kept because it is the one the street view depends on. Likewise the house's 74'-0" leaves 0.7 ft of the parcel's 74.7-ft frontage to the south of it. INFERRED for 1904: a 1911 map, carried back because the building did not move (1888 photograph; HABS 1963).

derivation.reason: The four derivation methods re-derive from the 1835 files (data/traces/street_control.json, data/streets/1835.json); none reads the 1904 street grid. This position is the prairie_1800 parcel's NE corner moved 14.7 ft along the parcel's own north line, and the note carries every number of that sum so it can be recomputed by hand from data/street_grid/1904.json.

footprint.note: The ground-floor masonry outline, courtyard excluded: 34 points, about 7,054 sq ft, from HABS sheet 2's dimension strings (sheet 3 for the 99'-3" courtyard), checked against Sanborn 1911 sheet 28 (the house drawn as a stone courtyard plan with the coach house at the alley) and the 1888 photograph — T-1731's outline (data/research/glessner_house_1904_spec.json § footprint), converted from the building frame to metres: x = (161.25 - W) * 0.3048, y = (74 - S) * 0.3048. The courtyard projections (stair tower, hall bow, dining bay) are measured, +/- 0.5 ft; printed runs +/- 0.1 ft.

value.W: feet west of the Prairie Avenue (east) face
value.S: feet south of the E. 18th Street (north) face

frame_ft.note: THE BUILDING FRAME every other attribute here is written in: HABS IL-1015's own, the plans' frame with their north arrow pointing down the sheet. 161'-3" along 18th Street and 74'-0" on Prairie Avenue are printed on sheet 2. Heights are in feet above one of two datums, named with each value: `door` is sheet 6's '0.00 AT DOOR' (the front-door sill), and the sidewalk before the doorway is printed at -0.74, so a door-datum height stands 0.74 ft higher above the walk; `ng` is the grade sheet 4 draws at the 18th Street wall. generators/archetypes/masonry_house_params.py converts all of them to metres once, into the footprint's frame (origin at the SW corner of the house's bounding box, x east, y north). T-2978: the court-face heights read on sheet 4 at T-2228's controls (zero y 5858) are heights over the court lawn the sheet draws under the east wing's court face, not over its ground at the 18th Street wall (y 5991, 1.36 ft lower); the model lays that lawn on `ng`. The sheets bound the lawn at 0 to +1.25 ft over the 18th Street grade and do not fix it (docs/RESEARCH/glessner-section-datum-T-2978/). L-glessner-court-fall-2978.

grade_datum.note: Sheet 4's 18th Street grade stands 0.20 ft over the Prairie Avenue sidewalk (sheet 6's -0.74), read off sheet 5 with its courses run level round the NE corner (T-2955): the Prairie elevation draws the printed course string (18, 18, 15.5 ... in) up from a base line 0.54 ft under the door sill, 0.20 ft over the walk, its beds at 0.92-7.58 ft against the string's 0.96-7.50 (T-2949, docs/RESEARCH/glessner-entry-T-2853/T-2913.md), and the 1888 photograph a18-gh-glessner-front-with-keith shows the same joints; the 18th Street elevation sets its apertures on that string's sums above its own grade (L305). One coursing serves both faces and its beds meet at the corner, so its base is one height: the 18th Street grade, 0.20 ft over the walk. No sheet prints the offset; it is inferred from the two elevations' coursing, inside T-1731's agreement of about a foot where they overlap. The committed heightfield is flat across the lot to 2 cm (e1871_postfire, 4.32-4.34 m) and is not re-cut for 6 cm: the walls still start at the walk, and the bottom course runs down to it.

construction.note: Street walls of rock-faced granite ashlar in alternating high and low courses over brick (Glessner 1923; HABS data pp. 20-21, sheet 5); courtyard walls of common brick with limestone lintels and sills. THE STONE'S NAME IS DISPUTED and is carried, not resolved: 'Wellesley granite' (Glessner 1923; HABS 1963) against 'Braggville pink granite' (the museum, per the Prairie library dossier G02). Neither reading changes the geometry.

paint.note: Bare masonry: nothing records a painted or limewashed surface on the house, and the 1888 photograph shows the dressed stone itself. `stone` is the value renderers/web/js/facades.js reads as masonry (jitter only, no silvering).

roof_covering.note: Red baked terracotta tiles, unglazed (Glessner 1923), about 6 in wide with 5 in exposed (HABS data p. 21, 1963, when they had been tar-covered; the tar is later than 1904 and excluded). The ridges are crested with raised tiles at about 1.16 ft centres (sheet 6; the 1888 photograph), which the mesh draws as a plain ridge roll.

granite_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. A pale pinkish grey. No colour source was read: the 1888 photograph is monochrome and shows a pale stone, and 'pink granite' is the museum's phrase as the Prairie library records it (G02). Bounded by the pale value of the 1888 plate and the pinkish name. HABS photograph 1 (1963) shows the same walls near black with soot; how far that had gone by 1904 is unknown and is not drawn.

brick_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. 'Common brick of slightly pinkish colour' is attested for the courtyard walls (Glessner 1923; HABS 1963); the tint itself is ours, a warm red-brown lifted toward pink. It is deliberately NOT the town's 1835 brick row (common/materials.py BRICK), which is a soft-mud brick argued off a different building.

trim_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. Grey Joliet limestone lintels and sills on the courtyard walls are attested (Glessner 1923; HABS 1963); the grey is ours. The same slot carries the copings, the voussoir rings and the carved tympanum over the front door.

roof_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. 'Red baked terracotta tiles, unglazed' (Glessner 1923) states the colour family; the value is ours, a dull brick-red dimmed for seventeen Chicago winters.

copper_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. Copper sheathing on the hall bow's roof is recorded by HABS (1963); by 1904 it had weathered for seventeen years in coal smoke, so it is drawn a dark brown rather than new copper or a full green patina. Also used for finials and the dining bay's faceted roof (see bay_dining_elevation).

wood_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. The porte-cochere and front doors are oak (the c. 1888 photograph; HABS data p. 21), and their finish is not recorded; a dark oiled oak is ours. The stable's carriage doors and the courtyard gate take the same slot.

range_east_wing.note: The Prairie Avenue range: 74'-0" along Prairie by 26'-6" (sheet 2), two storeys over a raised basement with an attic under a steep N-S gable (Sanborn '2B'; sheets 4, 6). Street faces granite; its courtyard (west) face brick (sheet 2 hatching; Glessner 1923). The south face is drawn granite on the evidence of sheet 4's stipple — Sanborn prints 'WALL B.' inside it, recorded and not interpreted. Its west wall north of the north range's courtyard face is inside the house and is not drawn.

ridge_east_wing.note: Heights retain sheet6's printed-datum reading: eave27.1 and ridge45.7 ft above door; west eave26.5 ft ng from sheet4. T-2470 supersedes the assumed W13.25 centreline: HABS01 and14 place the north gable crest at about W18.8 relative to sheet3's two window pairs. The gable spreads into the north range, with its western foot reconstructed at W37.6 and a concealed roof transition returning to the courtyard pitch by S14.6. There is no HABS north elevation or surveyed roof plan. Crest placement is photographically inferred; the rear transition is reconstructed. See L295. T-2228 supersedes the courtyard wall-plane eave: HABS4 visible roof edge y3188 is27.33ft above grade5858 at97.7px/ft. Continuing the retained ridge over the20cm overhang requires wall-plane28.83ft (rounded; +/-0.15ft source reading). The north facade retains its prior26.5ft datum and returns to this courtyard pitch within the existing concealed shoulder. Main ridge/east pitch unchanged; this reconciliation is reconstructed, not a printed survey dimension.

gable_east_wing_north.note: A stone parapet gable facing 18th Street, its coping rising from the eave corners to a chimney centred on the apex (1888 photograph; sheet 6 in profile; HABS photograph 1, 1963). The parapet's height above the roof (1.2 ft) is read off the 1888 plate against the eave, within about half a foot. T-2214: the coping stops at the stack's two sides and the parapet does not rise in front of it: between them the gable's wall stops at the stack's base and the stack's own face, flush with it, rises in its place carrying the datestones, as sheet 6 and HABS photograph 4 (cited, nothing derived) show the 18th Street gable. T-3024: the parapet stands 0.5 ft above its roof, where the 1888 plate's reading had 1.2 ft (+/- 0.5): HABS sheet 6 draws the coping meeting the stack's east side at about 43.7-43.9 ft above grade, 0.3-0.75 ft under the built 44.2-44.5, and through their cameras, with the stack's printed crest (48.62 ft door) as the anchor, HABS photograph 14 reads the coping meeting both of its sides 1.2-1.5 ft lower and both rakes 0.6-1.0 ft lower along their length, and HABS photograph 1 about 0.8 ft lower. Lowered 0.7 ft, the middle of the three, the coping now meets the stack just under the 1886 stone's foot, as all three show it. See L-glessner-stack-layout-3024.

gable_east_wing_south.note: Sheet 4 draws the south gable edge-on in stipple (stone) rising to about ridge height, and sheet 6 draws its coping at the south end of the Prairie slope; so a parapet gable to match the north one. In 1904 the three-storey house at 1808 (Sanborn '3B') stood against most of it — that house is T-0475's, not drawn here.

range_north_range.note: The E. 18th Street range between the east wing (W 26.5) and the stable (W 125.75), 26'-10" deep (1'-7" + 4'-1" + 1'-8" + 18'-0" + 1'-6", sheet 2), two storeys over the basement (Sanborn '2B'). Granite to the street, brick to the courtyard. Its west end (about W 96.5-125.75) is the service block, entered 'through the great arch on Eighteenth Street' (Glessner 1923). The roof is drawn running into the east wing's and the stable's (to W 20 and W 139), under their slopes, so the valleys are the true intersections; its courtyard wall behind the hall bow is inside the house. V4: continue the north-range roof to the measured alley plane W 161.25, through the stable roof. HABS photograph 1 shows both the stable north gable and a ridge continuing behind it toward the alley; the owner's supplied modern overview confirms the cross-gabled reading qualitatively. The roof extension is inferred from the unchanged masonry envelope and the two intersecting ranges, rather than traced from the modern image. The alley triangular closure is declared in v4_detail.

ridge_north_range.note: Sheet 4 (Section A-A, cut at W 51.3): ridge 34.1 ft above north grade, 14.6 ft south of the street face; street eave 23.1 ft, courtyard eave 26.5 ft; 36.6 degrees both ways, the courtyard slope flattening to about 27 degrees over its lowest 5.7 ft. The section is the only cut, and the profile is carried the length of the range on the evidence of the 1888 photograph (the 18th Street eave running level from the east gable to the stable's) and HABS photograph 1 (1963: one straight ridge from the east wing to the stable). T-2016: retain the section ridge/eave control points but replace the earlier kicked interpretation with one planar courtyard slope, directed by the owner aerial review. The prior measured section interpretation is preserved in the research spec; this planar interpolation is reconstructed. T-2183: the owner reports the missing courtyard awning. HABS photograph 05 and the supplied detail show a projecting eave continuous with the dining-bay roof edge, not a separate fabric canopy. Extend only the courtyard overhang to S29.19 (2.36 ft beyond its wall, matching the existing bay shoulders), and set its outer edge to 24.0 ft ng, meeting the bay roof base. With the existing S14.6/z34.1 ridge and a planar slope, the wall-line roof ordinate is 25.633722 ft ng, replacing the prior 26.5-ft extrapolation at this junction. The upper ridge and street eave stay fixed. Projection and junction ordinate are reconstructed (+/-0.5 ft), bounded by the measured bay plan and the photographed continuous eave; they are not asserted as a printed HABS dimension.

range_west_wing.note: The coach house — stable, carriage room, harness room and hay loft with the coachmen's rooms over — 35'-6" E-W by 59'-9" N-S at the alley (sheets 2-3), 1 1/2 storeys over the furnace room (Sanborn '1 1/2'; Glessner 1923: heating 'from the furnace room under the garage'). Granite on 18th Street and the alley; brick on its courtyard and south faces (sheet 2 hatching). ITS 1904 USE is inferred to be the stable it was built as: Glessner in 1923 writes 'the carriage house and stables (now garage)', and Sanborn labels it GARAGE in 1911, but nothing read dates the conversion before 1904. The exterior is the same either way.

ridge_west_wing.note: SETTLED BY HABS PHOTOGRAPH 1 (Cervin Robinson, 23 July 1963, 'exterior from northwest'), which T-1731 had not read and which replaces the spec's reconstructed 45-degree symmetric roof. On that print the gable apex, the loft opening and the carriage doorway stand on one axis, and sheet 2 prints the doorway at W 134.9-147.0, so the RIDGE is at W 141.0 (centre of the doorway), not at the wing's centre line (W 143.5). Scaled off the same print against the printed 12'-0" doorway (13.3-13.5 px/ft at the stable face): gable coping apex about 39.6 ft above grade, so the ridge about 38.6 ft; the west eave at the NW corner about 26.3 ft; the east slope comes down to the 18th Street eave line at 23.1 ft, which the 1888 photograph shows running level into the foot of this gable. Tolerance about 1.5 ft on each height (a 1963 oblique photograph). The pitches that follow are about 41 degrees east and 31 west. Carried to 1904 because the 1946 alteration list (HABS data p. 2) names no roof work and the 1888 photograph shows the same gable and turret. Richardson's side-elevation sketch GLE B9 (Houghton; design intent, NOT evidence of the as-built form) draws the same gable centred on the carriage doorway.

gable_west_wing_north.note: A stone parapet gable on 18th Street with a relieving arch of radiating voussoirs over the loft opening (1888 photograph; HABS photograph 1). The coping stands about 1 ft above the roof line on the 1963 print.

gable_west_wing_west.note: T-3096: the alley gable is a parapet gable. Both the c. 1887 Cornell print and HABS photograph 1 draw a stone coping standing proud along its rakes with its apex up at the cresting, where the roof behind it comes down (T-3095, docs/RESEARCH/glessner-stable-ridge-T-3095/ section 3). The wall keeps its apex where it stood (stable_roof_rework.alley_gable_apex, S 14.6 at 38.6 ft ng, so the coping's top at about 40.2 ft, inside T-2758's 38.75-40.63 ft read through the two Cornell fits); the 1-ft rise of its coping over the wall line is the 18th Street gable's on the same stable, carried here: INFERRED, not read on the alley face.

gable_west_wing_south.note: The stable's south end (toward the courtyard's alley end and 1808's rear yard) is not drawn or photographed in anything read. Sheet 2 draws its south wall in brick. A plain brick gable matching the north end's roof is the simplest reading; a hip is equally possible. docs/LIBERTIES.md L295. T-1830 supersedes the former full-height gable with a hipped rear roof, bounded by the lower west eave and sheet-3 upper openings. The upper windows remain exposed beneath its 23.1-ft eave; the c.1955 external wooden stair remains excluded.

tower_stair.note: The round stair tower on the east wing's courtyard face: centre and radius measured on sheet 2 (+/- 0.5 ft), wall top 32.5 and cone apex 42.3 ft above north grade on sheet 4. HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923, the court) shows it: brick, conical roof, finial. The eave's half-foot overhang is the drawing's (sheet 4). T-2228 uses the independently rectified HABS2 plan centreS56.0989ft, rounded56.1, superseding55.0. W27.3/r5.25 remain. T-2879 ruled the plan against sheet 4: the printed court chain on sheet 2 puts the tower's 10'-0" mass at S51.33-61.33, and r5.25 at W27.3 meets the W26.5 face at S50.91-61.29. Sheet 4's 11.09-ft drum, re-zeroed +0.65 ft on the printed court face, runs S51.86-62.95 and overruns that mass, so sheet 4 draws the drum wide; its S56.73/r5.55 is not adopted for position or radius, and its tower heights are unaffected (docs/RESEARCH/glessner-court-ruling-T-2879/). Roof heights remain under section review. T-2228 supersedes old roof heights with HABS4 grade5858/97.7px per ft: eavey2613=33.214ft, bell base1858=40.942ft and top1683=42.733ft. Hidden cone apex41.60ft extrapolates straight side slopes beneath the bell and is reconstructed. Court-specific finial silhouette replaces the generic finial.

tower_north.note: T-2470: HABS 01/13/14 show a flat north gable continuing into a west half-round drum, not an exposed complete cylinder. The photograph-bounded eave/apex are 33.3/43.4 ft ng, with a 1.5-ft finial. The sheet-4 section shows the tower beyond its cutting plane and does not establish its circular plan; the old full-cylinder interpretation is superseded. The total cone rise is 10.1 ft, including a reconstructed 1.1-ft bellcast skirt, within the approximately one-foot uncertainty of the 10.32-ft sheet reading. These are photographic proportions, not new surveyed dimensions. See docs/RESEARCH/glessner-north-tower-T-2470.md and L295.

tower_north_plan.note: T-2470: reconstruct W41/S7.35, radius7.35 ft, with the north tangent on the 18th Street wall and only the west half curved. The north gable continues flat from W0 to W41. HABS 01/13/14 and the sheet-3 window spacings supersede L295's earlier W35 +/-3-ft estimate, which incorrectly assumed a freestanding cylinder. The 9.35-ft eave radius includes the photographed flare. Sheet4 is a section, not a roof plan; these coordinates remain reconstructed. The HABS01 camera excludes the tower from its fit. The independently reconciled HABS14 camera is held fixed across before/after, with remaining residual recorded honestly. L295 addendum.

hall_bow.note: T-2218: HABS sheet 2's printed 161 ft 3 in / 74 ft envelope calibrates the scan independently. Its printed 9 ft 6 in radius is the INSIDE bow; the measured outer wall is about 10.6 ft (±0.2 ft), centred W27.8/S28.8 (±0.25 ft). The previous W28/S27.7, R10.1 reading displaced the terrace/stair interface. This corrects that shared boundary without changing the approved central door, threshold height or light rows. Measured 1963 fabric is inferred for 1904; HABS photo 05 is a qualitative cross-check only. T-2879: sheet 2 prints 12'-6" from the range's court face (26'-10", S26.83) to the bow's tangent on the east wing face (S39.33), which places the bow where it is built; sheet 4 draws it 12.45 ft across, shifted 0.65 ft north with the court face, not rescaled. See docs/RESEARCH/glessner-courtyard-steps-T-2218.md and docs/RESEARCH/glessner-court-ruling-T-2879/.

hall_bow_height.note: Two storeys to the courtyard eave (26.5 ft, sheet 4): sheet 4 draws the bow beyond its section plane with its wall top at the eave line, and HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923) shows it, brick with stone lintels and sills, three lights to a storey, rising to the eave of the east wing's courtyard slope. The light rows are the house's own first- and second-floor window heights (sheets 4-5). T-2228 re-reading of native HABS4 at the fixed shared ground datum places the bow eave at (5858-3188)/97.7=27.33ft ng, superseding26.5. This is a scaled1963fabric reading inferred for1904, ±0.15ft, not a printed height. Light rows and door threshold stay at their independent controls. T-2925 reads the bow's lights, door and stone courses on the native sheet-4 scan (grade y 5858, north wall x 1165, 100.6/97.7 px/ft; docs/RESEARCH/glessner-court-exterior-T-2925/) and carries their S onto the plan's frame by T-2879's +0.65 ft, which puts the drawn bow's flanks (S26.21-38.66) on the built ones. Sheet 4 draws a light by its extent along S, so each is set on the arc where its edges project there (lights_S): above, two broad lights at S29.08-32.56 and 34.27-36.83 and a narrow one at 37.80-38.69; below, a broad light at 29.10-32.59, the garden door at 34.38-36.83 and a narrow light at 37.86-38.69 - the door one storey under the middle light, as before, and no longer three equal lights spread evenly round the arc. Openings run from sill to lintel: 9.05-14.20 ft below (was 9.3-14.5) and 19.45-24.29 above (was 19.5-24.0); the door's foot stays on the terrace deck, behind the coping the section draws at 8.43 ft. The lintels and the upper sill are drawn as continuous stone courses from S28.76 to the bow's south flank (S39.27): 14.20-15.49 and 24.29-25.62 ft lintels, an 18.72-19.45 ft sill; the lower sills are two stones under the lights either side of the door (stone_courses). Each edge +/-0.05 ft (about 5 px). A 1963 measured drawing carried to 1904 fabric, so the confidence stays inferred.

hall_bow_roof.note: HABS data p. 21 (1963): 'The roof of the bow of the entrance hall in the ell of the house is covered with copper sheathing' — the material is carried to 1904 (nothing records a change). Its full roof plan is not drawn: sheet 4 shows a short low roof over the bow meeting the main slopes. The earlier 3.5-ft cone-sector reconstruction (L295) is superseded by T-2220: the native sheet-4 section gives approximately 174 px at 97.7 px/ft, a relative hood rise of 1.78 ft (+/- 0.17 ft). Use 1.8 ft above the retained 26.5-ft bow eave, with its high point at the actual courtyard ell W26.5/S26.83 (the section reads S26.81 +/- 0.12 ft). Clip the low hood into both adjoining tiled slopes; there is no broad copper rectangle over the north windows. The absolute section/eave datum disagreement remains in the T-2228 comparison. Individual seams and 1904 patina remain reconstructed, not measured original sheet stock. See L-glessner-copper-2220. Modern surviving-form cross-checks only: wlemay_glessner_courtyard_2024_159537053, wlemay_glessner_courtyard_2024_159537081 and wlemay_glessner_courtyard_2024_159537087; no later colour or fitting is promoted to a 1904 fact. T-2228 raises only the shared bow eave to27.33ft ng from the native section; relative1.8ft rise is retained and both host intersections are regenerated. T-2861: sheet 4's section (native scan, T-2228's controls) ends the hood's copper at S38.62, plan S39.27 after T-2879's +0.65 ft, on the bow wall's drawn face (S38.66, plan 39.31; built 39.4): the hood does not oversail the wall. The eave is set 0.05 ft past the built wall face (was 0.20 m, which ended the hood at about S39.9), so its 45 mm drip apron stands clear of the brick and inside the trough. The hood's silhouette on habs04-hood-section now ends at the bow wall's, 0.09 ft south of the drawn line, which is T-2925's carried bow-radius difference, not the hood's.

bay_dining.note: The dining-room bay on the north range's courtyard face: five facets, 19.4 ft wide, projecting 10.3 ft (sheet 2; the room inside printed 17'-8" x 11'-0").

bay_dining_elevation.note: SETTLED IN FORM BY HABS PHOTOGRAPH 5 (a c. 1923 view of the court from The Story of a House), where T-1731 had a one-storey bay 'roofed below the second-floor windows' from sheet 3 alone. The photograph shows the bay as a masonry storey of large lights with a stone band at the second-floor level, over it a continuous glazed band of multi-pane sash, and a tall faceted roof of seamed sheet metal rising into the north range's slope. Sheet 3's light, many-sided outline at the second floor agrees: a glazed band drawn as joinery, not masonry. The HEIGHTS are read off the print against the adjoining wall's floor levels (sheet 4: second floor 17.4 ft), within about 1.5 ft: band top 20.5 ft in v4; the faceted roof's point at the height of the north range's ridge (34.0 ft), where the print puts it, standing on the slope 6.8 ft behind the wall. Phase: a 1923 photograph, carried to 1904 because the 1892 changes were interior and nothing records exterior work before 1946. The roof metal is drawn in the copper slot; its material is not stated. V4 re-reads the full-resolution photograph: the glazed band is about 78 px high against 129 px for the 5.2-ft main sash, implying about 3.1 ft above the 17.4-ft masonry. Its 20.5-ft top replaces the default’s inferred 23-ft reading, with approximately 1-ft uncertainty. The band has two glazed pane rows with a horizontal rail, rather than floor-height single sheets. T-2016: the apex meets the north ridge at S14.6/z34.1; the two rear return facets are tiled, as HABS courtyard photograph 05 shows. The hip and two flanking tiled valleys are clipped into the host slope rather than overlaid. T-2157 supersedes the T-2016 apex placement: the copper hip ends over the bay shoulders at S29.19, retaining z34.1 and W70.6. A level tiled cross ridge joins it to the north ridge at S14.6, with the same raised terracotta collars. The main roof retains its eave and is cut only along the true intersection valleys. The hip has a shallow flared copper apron. This is reconstructed from the owner-supplied aerial and March 2023 detail, bounded by the existing HABS plan and roof heights; exact apron and seam dimensions are not measured 1904 fabric. T-2172 supersedes the 17.4/20.5-ft band placement: the owner courtyard photograph and HABS photograph 5 show the upper glazing at the adjoining north-wing upper-window level. Keep the historically divided, 3.1-ft-high sash band and lift it 3.5 ft to 20.9-24.0 ft ng, aligning its head to the existing north-court second-floor window heads. The masonry extends to its new sill; the basement openings remain fixed. The unchanged 34.1-ft ridge makes the copper cap 10.1 ft tall rather than 13.6 ft. These heights are reconstructed alignment estimates (+/-1 ft), not a survey transcription; the modern replacement undivided panes are not carried into 1904. The principal sash heads rise from 14.5 to 16.5 ft, retaining 9.3-ft sills, facet positions and divided sash. The supplied photo and HABS courtyard photo show the main lights approximately 2-2.5 times the upper band height; 7.2/3.1 = 2.32 gives that proportion and avoids an oversized blank brick spandrel after raising the band. This is reconstructed, approximately +/-1 ft, not a printed HABS dimension. The museum's 2013 post 'The stone capitals on Glessner House' (glessnerhouse.blogspot.com, 2013-02-11; three close-ups held as a18-ghm-blog-capital-*) records nine capitals, front and north, carved in place from August 1887 by John Evans of Evans & Tomb, each different, the one over the front door carrying Richardson's monogram; its close-ups give the block's form (straight-sided under the band, rounded in to the shaft below), the neck at about 0.55 of the block's width and the capital about 0.9 of its width tall. Shaft: 0.68 ft at the neck and 0.9 ft at the foot, between the sheet's outlines (0.63 / 0.9) and the close-ups' neck-to-block ratio, its taper what the c. 1888 front (a18-gh-glessner-front-with-keith) shows. Heights are shares of the record's opening, which since T-2985 is the 5.1 ft sheet 6 draws (it was 4.5 ft), so the base stands about 0.66 ft and the capital 1.5 ft, as the sheet draws them. Sheet 3 (second-floor plan, 37.3 px/ft on its 161'-3") cuts each as a round-fronted stone mullion about 0.95 ft wide and 1.5 ft deep, its round face on the wall's face and the sashes meeting its back. Taylor 2135 and the close-ups show the colonnettes in the walls' own granite. The motifs are read from the pictures; their cuts, depths and the four capitals no close-up shows are reconstructed (LIBERTIES).

v4_detail.note: V4 detail schedule. Stable courtyard and south upper opening horizontal bounds are measurements from sheets 2-3, rounded to half-foot-scale accuracy; their heights and the unrecorded garden/south lower lights are reconstructed. East court garden light and bow basement pair are visible on sheet 4; dining garden lights are visible in photograph 5. Cross-gable roof dimensions use the canonical ranges and the HABS footprint; the smaller alley dormer, the copper return and chimney-flue layouts are reconstructed forms, bounded by the owner's requested omissions and surviving fabric comparisons without tracing modern imagery. T-2220 supersedes the former pitched north-range return with a low copper hood intersected with both tiled roof slopes; the unused rectangular-return controls are removed. Full per-feature evidence and uncertainty: docs/RESEARCH/glessner_house_v4.md. Surface joint width and relief are artistic reconstructions; they are not survey measurements. docs/LIBERTIES.md v4 entry. HABS photographs 14-15 also supply the omitted east-wing high arched slit and the stable gable's 5-3-1 pigeon-hole arrangement and ledge. Their dimensions are reconstructed photographic proportions (+/- 1 ft), not survey labels. Joinery recesses, sash widths, carved detail depths and grille thicknesses are reconstructed; the Prairie basement 3-by-3 stone grilles and the porte-cochere's two leaves with 3-by-6 panels each are attested by sheets 5-6 and the c.1888 door photograph. The 7-by-7 front door iron grid is a simplified reconstruction of the denser grille shown on sheet 5. The stair tower has four staggered slit windows and an upper three-light front lantern row, heights measured from sheet 4 (+/-1 ft); angles/widths are reconstructed on the measured drum. A low projecting bowed terrace carries TWO basement grilles and a main-level central door, as sheet 4/photo 5 show. Terrace radius 14 ft and coping dimensions are reconstructed. The underpass is an actual opening through the east range with stone returns, its plan bounds from sheet 2 and entrance heads from sheets 4/6; it is not an opaque dark panel. Later owner views image(9), image(10), and the courtyard westward view received 2026-09-29 confirm those distinctions qualitatively. That westward view also resolves the stable upper windows as nearly square, not transoms: z18–22.5 with the sheet3 widths; lower narrow lights z7.5–13.5. These unprinted heights remain reconstructed. The historical paired porte-cochere leaves are posed 82 degrees inward, a reconstructed momentary operating position chosen to reveal the full passage; their documented construction is retained. Modern images inform feature arrangement, counts and material boundaries where explicitly named; no photographed pixels are reused. The modern courtyard image(9) refines the reconstructed bow-terrace grille height to z 1–3.8 ft ng (beneath a 6.1-ft platform) and dining garden lights to z 1–5 ft ng; these are proportion estimates, not HABS dimensions. Image(10) also supports a parapet above the walking platform that partly hides the central door. Its 2.2-ft height (about 0.67 m, bounded 0.55–0.8 m) is a proportional reconstruction; nine risers are reconstructed from the 1.68-m rise, not counted in the partially visible photograph. The doorway threshold aligns with the platform. HABS photograph 5 and supplied courtyard image(9) show garden grilles alternating beneath the principal dining-bay sash: three openings on normalized principal facets 0, 2 and 4, with brick beneath facets 1 and 3. The tower lantern retains the six-pane (2 columns by 3 rows) lights visible in HABS photograph 5, rather than the replacement 1-over-1 sash in modern views. The raised north-court service door has the landing and south-descending stair drawn on HABS sheet 2. Plan bounds are scaled against the four-foot door, approximately +/- 0.5 ft; the ten risers and three-foot rail are reconstructed. Stone slab/treads, two slender brick landing supports, a brick stair cheek and iron rail are bounded by the supplied tunnel-facing courtyard photograph, not claimed as measured original details. This is separate from the later wooden stairs outside the stable south wall. T-1805: HABS photographs 1 and 15 show the stable north gable returning to the north-range eave BEFORE the alley corner. The former full-width asymmetric triangle was a misreading. The north gable is reconstructed between W 125.75 and 156.25, centered on the existing W 141 loft/door/pigeon axis, with both feet at the north-range eave z 23.1 ft ng. The remaining 5 ft to W 161.25 continues that eave. These feet have about 1 ft photographic uncertainty. The rear tie-in to the unchanged stable roof is a bounded continuous reconstruction inside the crossing north-range roof; it is not a surveyed roof plan. No opening is moved to accommodate the old incorrect slope. T-1830 supersedes T-1805's continuous interpolated roof and unchanged rear profile. The full west-facing northern gable returns to the lower alley eave at S32; the rear range is asymmetric with a hipped south end. Cross ridge 34.1, rear ridge 31, west eave 15.5, east/south eaves 23.1 ft ng are bounded reconstructions, about +/-1.5 ft where not measured. The measured north-range section is preserved at the east join with a planar valley connector. The west dormer is timber with tile cheeks and a hipped projecting hood, not a stone miniature gable. Roof planes are clipped at their actual intersections. The north porch is a 12-ft arch, 6-ft-deep reconstructed recess, 3 front risers and 8 left-turn risers to the 6-ft raised threshold; plan footprint and side-door arrangement are checked against sheets 2–3, unprinted tread heights and window heights remain reconstructed. See L-glessner-courtyard-ridge-2235. T-2203 roof tiles: HABS IL-1015 data printed p. 21 (PDF p. 22) records six-inch width and five-inch exposure. T-2205: closed ridge caps, moulded terminal seats, eave fascia/soffit stock and valley/abutment flashing are reconstructed sections. T-2211 street and stable sash: HABS photograph 14 shows the east-wing gable's high light as a glazed round head in its own arched frame, a stone transom, and a one-over-one sash below (the c. 1923 HABS photograph 4, cited as a cross-check only, agrees). T-2214: the 18th Street stack's AD monogram over 1886 is read from HABS photograph 4 (c. 1923 copy; cited, nothing derived): both are incised, read left to right from the street (the glyphs had advanced eastward, which from the street is right to left: a mirrored date), and two incised crosses flank the date. The stones stand 0.06 m proud of the stack's own face, now flush with the gable (see chimneys), at the heights sheet 6 draws them (43.6-45.5 and 45.8-47.2 ft ng, about 0.2 ft proud); their widths (W 11.7-14.8 and 11.85-14.65) are photograph 4's shares of the stack's 5.1-ft face, the lettering spans its read share of each stone, and the crosses sit midway in the margins, about 0.6 ft across (T-3024 levels them at the date stone's mid-height; they had stood 28 % and 70 % up it, read off photograph 4's upward view). Letterforms are a generic face standing in for the carver's, and the cut is drawn as a dark stroke on the face. See L-glessner-datestone-2214. T-2870: HABS photograph 14 (1965; no known restrictions, so derived from) reads the upper stone's monogram as one joined device, not two letters: two bowls facing outward, each closed by a stem, with a bar between the stems at mid-height. It is now drawn as those strokes (ad_device), not set in a font: about 0.43 of the stone's width and 0.53 of its height, centred, the stems at 0.33 and 0.73 of its width and the stroke 0.16 of its height, read at the photograph's grain (the device is about 32 px across). That the device is the carver's A and D, as photograph 4 reads it, is the earlier reading; its interlacing finer than the print shows is not drawn. prairie_frontage.note: T-2202. House-side lawn edging and access gaps are visible in Taylor 2135 (c.1887–89) and HABS sheets 2/6 (1963/1965); continuity in 1904 is inferred, not a dated survey. The 14.7-ft setback reuses the existing Sanborn-aligned placement; the final 1.02 ft crosses only the reconstructed public margin to meet T-1728's unchanged six-foot walk. Curbs stop at the main entry and porte and return to the house with rounded plan corners and dressed top edges. Profile height 1.05 ft, width 0.65 ft, 0.8-ft corner radius and 4-ft joint spacing are bounded reconstructions (+/-0.25 ft profile, +/-1.5 ft setback), not dimensions printed by HABS. The door sill retains sheet 6's 0.00 datum, 0.74 ft above its sidewalk; two low stone risers join the existing sill to the rendered approach. The rendered 0.21-ft paving lift includes the terrain/sidewalk display clearance, not a newly surveyed historical grade. Passage paving tapers to the existing 0.12-ft courtyard drive, with no grass or duplicated floor. Paving uses dressed stone at the entry and neutral mineral surfacing at the carriage approach/passage; historic composition and joint layout remain reconstructed. No later street pavement is imported. L-glessner-frontage-2202. T-2228 supersedes the two risers: one continuous broad threshold is built into the cutback entry at the retained sill datum. Approach/curb gap widens to9.6ft to clear the9.1ft threshold, bounded by HABS5 and the owner photograph; one6.36in rendered rise above the display-lifted approach. No added projecting upper tread. T-2976 supersedes the passage paving lift: the carriage passage's floor is sunk, as both HABS sheets draw it. Sheet 6 (read at its own printed 0.00 and 24.30, 75.3 px/ft) runs the porte-cochere's opening and both oak leaves down to 1.9 ft under the door datum, 1.16 ft under the sidewalk it prints at -0.74, the sidewalk line returning down into the opening at both jambs; sheet 4 draws the court mouth's floor 1.05 ft (103 px at 97.7 px/ft) under the court ground drawn beside it. So passage_front_z is the sheet-6 floor and passage_court_z is that depth under the model's 0.12-ft court drive. (T-2955: the court drive lies on the model's grade, not on north grade, so that depth is written on the door datum, -1.67 ft = -0.93 ft over the model's grade, and does not rise with the 18th Street grade.) With the floor where the sheets put it the passage clears 8.9 ft under the street head (sheet 6: 7.0 over the door datum) and 8.15 ft under the court lintel, against 7.0 ft when it was laid at the display-lifted sidewalk. The c.1888 photograph agrees: its leaves run down past the rounded stones at the jambs' feet. The carriage approach across the setback now falls from the walk to the sunk mouth (1.37 ft over about 15 ft), with a dressed stone retaining edge up to the ground along each side; where and how the 1904 approach fell is not drawn, so its line, fall and edging are reconstructed (docs/LIBERTIES.md L-glessner-passage-floor-2976). T-2978: passage_court_z is the court mouth opening's foot as sheet 4 draws it, 2.45 ft under the court face's zero (y 6097 against y 5858 at 97.7 px/ft) and 1.02 ft under the ground drawn beside the mouth, which the court's fall now lays: the passage clears 9.67 ft under the court lintel (sheet 9.65) and the floor falls 1.1 ft from the street mouth. L-glessner-court-fall-2978.

rainwater_details.note: T-2221 / L-glessner-rainwater-2221: early Taylor shows framed Prairie rainwater heads and broad wall straps; unrestricted HABS01/14 locate the small service collector and ribbed north-tower bowl. Later fabric corroborates routing, not exact 1904 fittings. Head dimensions, unreadable low-relief ornament, 3 mm stock, 105 mm rectangular leaders, 180 by 140 mm box gutters, concealed court branches and discharge fittings are bounded reconstructions. Licensed modern courtyard photos constrain box sections only; bright green patina and modern inspection caps are excluded. Upper tower leader enters the lower bowl rather than ending above the roof; all gutter edges inherit existing roof planes. Head camera fit is relative to retained geometry, not independent survey. Unresolved absolute eave/grade correspondence remains T-2228. Prairie strap centres at 1.74, 4.07 and 6.30 m fit the fixed Taylor camera at display y825,700,580; they are model-based estimates (about +/-0.08 m), not surveyed elevations. Bow and dining leaders alone use 160 by 100 mm fluted box stock with broad 400 mm straps, bounded by licensed modern courtyard close-ups relative to brick courses; their precise 1904 profiles remain reconstructed. Other concealed outlets retain plainer sections. Close-up comparison requires a separate matte grey-green oxidised/coated rainwater finish (linear RGB 0.085/0.095/0.090, roughness 0.72, metallic 0.15): this is bounded reconstruction, not a sampled 1904 colour or identified alloy. Existing iron hardware remains unchanged. The framed panel has 14 mm raised stock, 24 mm bead diameter and a plain boss 38 percent of head width; these resolve the early scan's broad relief without inventing a legible emblem. T-2228 locates the two east-court straight leaders at S61.61 and S42.4 ft, bounded reconstructions within the retained gutter fragments and the clear wall strips beside the revised tower and garden light. These are clearance-driven placements, not measurements of historic downpipes. They retain the existing stock and avoid both glazing and carriage openings; the south strip is narrow, with the existing straps checked independently. T-2926: sheet 4 draws the east court's south leader at the wing's south end, not beside the stair tower: its pipe at sheet S72.80-73.27, so S73.68 on the plan's frame (T-2879's +0.65 ft), under a hopper head 0.47 m across its top (S72.26-73.80) and 0.24 m deep in elevation (26.1-26.87 ft), tapering to the pipe. It hangs under the gutter, not up to its rim as the photographed heads do: its top is dropped 0.15 m, which the render read 0.5 ft above the drawn one. The hopper's depth off the wall is not drawn and is reconstructed at its width's half; the pipe keeps the existing stock (sheet 4 draws about 0.14 m against the built 0.105). Sheet 4 draws no leader at the north one's S42.4; it stays as T-2228 set it until T-2928 reads that strip. T-2928: sheet 4 draws no leader anywhere on the strip between the bow and the stair tower (S39-51, sheet frame): its eave gutter runs at 27.0-27.6 ft from the drum to the bow trough's drawn south end at S38.9-39.3. So the court-east-north leader and its straps are removed, and the strip's gutter is recorded as draining into the bow trough (court_east_into_bow). How it passes its water into the trough is not drawn; both ends keep their caps as built. T-2861: sheet 4 draws the bow's trough end-on at the bow's south end: its top at the hood's eave (27.38 ft), its face 0.31 ft (0.094 m) out from the wall line, its foot at 27.0-27.04 ft, so 0.34-0.38 ft (0.11 m) deep, and no separate fascia board under it - the brick runs up to the trough. bow_gutter carries that section on the bow only, its outlet at the trough's middle; the trough's moulding and stock stay reconstructed. Was the shared 0.18 m x 0.14 m box hung outside a 0.20 m hood overhang, its face about 1.13 ft out from the wall. T-2939: sheet 4 draws the court-bow leader side-on, not face-on. Its back runs down the north range's court face (S26.2, sheet frame) and its front at S26.53, so the pipe stands in the corner with the bow, on that wall, 0.33 ft (0.10 m) deep: the 100 mm side of the 160 x 100 mm stock, whose broad fluted face therefore looks south into the court. Under the trough's floor (27.04 ft) hangs a head 0.75 ft (0.229 m) deep off the wall, straight-fronted down to 26.56 ft and its front then stepping in to the pipe's 0.10 m by 25.8 ft: the line T-2861 read as the pipe offsetting north is that head's front, its back staying on the wall. Two thin circles are drawn on the head's side: a ring 0.37 ft across centred at S26.47, 26.37 ft and a stud 0.12 ft across at S26.72, 26.71 ft; both are built as shallow round bosses (bow_leader.studs) because the drawing does not say what they are. The head's width along the wall is not drawn and is the pipe's plus its stock (0.172 m); its stock, its fixing and what the ring is stay reconstructed. The drop from the trough's outlet into the head is inside the head. Was a face-on box leader on the bow wall, 0.16 m along S, its outlet dropping straight down 0.09 m and then offsetting 0.3 ft south to the bow's face, with no head and no ring.

stack_finish.note: T-2222 / L-glessner-stacks-2222: HABS sheets 4/6 show a broad stone top course and shallower course below on the street stacks, corroborated qualitatively by early Taylor. 448 mm top-course height and 229 mm lower bed are raster-bounded estimates, not surveyed stock; 320 mm cap modules and 8 mm joints reconstruct unreadable return joints. Licensed 2024 w_lemay views distinguish two brick service shafts with plain pale stone caps; carrying that fabric into 1904 is explicitly reconstructed, not dated by modern photographs. Their existing presence, plans and heights are retained pending early evidence. Service caps use 220 mm stock and 450 mm bounded modules. All flue counts remain the prior unmeasured reconstructions (two, four or six mouths); 300 mm maximum mouth width, 600 mm brick-lined depth and 12 mm top drainage fall are invented within masonry construction bounds. No pots or repeated side vents are added. Every new finish face is reconstructed. Other roof, glazing and granite-colour choices are preserved. Light retains every shaft plane, cap thickness, exterior cap joint, mouth and flue depth. It omits only service shafts' 1–6 mm per-brick relief, fine internal top-bed cap joints and the interior flue lining material break; the same metric brick textures and dark masonry lining remain. The complete Light assembly measures 199,967 triangles against the unchanged 200,000 ceiling.

service_access_details.note: T-2223: retain the existing HABS sheet 2 north-court landing/flight plan, ten treads, 6-ft landing and 3-ft nominal guard. The separately labelled wooden stair behind the west/stable wing was added ca.1955 and remains excluded. The current courtyard stair is visible in 1963 and 2024; those sources do not independently date every member to 1904. Modern licensed frames bound two lower horizontal rails, sparse posts, brick cheek and brick piers with pale capitals. Exact rail stock, seated base plates, continuous return joins, capital bevels and buried footings are bounded reconstructions. The paired alley leaves follow the existing HABS plan opening, with the retained reconstructed 8-ft top; board joints, two ledges and a compression brace per leaf, dressed coursed gate reveals, plain two-hinge hardware, latch and flush sill are reconstructed, not traced from an undocumented elevation. Rendered ground measurements place the gate within 0.5 mm of ng and the ground beneath service piers about 15.4 mm below ng; buried bases close contact without moving the landing or gate top. No modern wrapping, paint, paving or plants are copied. Light omits only shallow brick relief on the stair cheek and support piers while retaining the same outlines, seated posts, cap profiles, rail runs, leaf gaps and connected hinge geometry. See the T-2223 component register and liberty. The sill is 50 mm stone stock, entering grade by 5 mm; the brick cheek starts at local datum and meets the existing raised lawn. Only the stone stair/pier footings extend to -40 mm. Hinge knuckles sit outside the timber ledges, tangent to their front faces, with straps meeting the exposed pins directly. The brick cheek follows each tread underside, beneath the stone noses; landing rails follow both exposed outer edges, and the latch passes through an open keeper.

vines_details.note: T-2225: seven bounded original planting studies for July 1904. HABS establishes wall locations and openings; the USDA guide supplies Virginia-creeper botanical bounds only, not Glessner planting history or coverage. Boston ivy profiles are independently drawn generic three-lobed botanical reconstructions. The species history remains separately cited in form.vines; its unresolved typescript and later-image rights are not cleared by this work and no image is traced or sampled. Two selective Prairie ivy areas and five courtyard creeper areas are reconstructed placement, scale, maintenance and growth, not a measured 1904 map. The south boundary, west wall and one north-wall pier carry creeper; window/door openings and their surrounds retain at least 220 mm clearance. No new neighborhood trees, flower beds or plants over unresolved tower/roof geometry. Mature leaves are green for July; conspicuous ripe berries and autumn colors are omitted. Seeded branches, root joints, curled lobed/compound leaves and a generated alpha atlas share one numeric layout. Light carries the same atlas on four connected panels per plant, collapsing leaf depth while preserving its visible coverage. Full stems follow actual masonry faces. Precise branch trajectories, leaf shapes, veins, serration, color, wall offsets and coverage remain liberties; better dated summer evidence should replace them.

surface_finish.note: T-2226: use the existing slightly pink courtyard clay, grey mortar and 215.9 by 66.675 mm half-bond course module on previously plain stair returns and Light stair/pier/boundary faces. The new original periodic maps represent existing joints without adding geometry or double-gridding modeled bricks. The 9 mm joint, 5 mm normal-map recess, fine edge transition and per-unit kiln variation are bounded render reconstructions, not measured 1904 samples. Oak grain follows each rear-gate ledge and compression brace at the existing physical texture scale; cut ends retain a nondegenerate generic oak study, not claimed measured end grain. Neutral diagnostic and actual July views preserve the owner grey-greige granite, dark glazing and existing lighting/contact geometry. No copied modern patina, neglected mid-century deterioration or invented directional grime is added: the 1923 family account describes unglazed red roof tiles, pinkish brick with grey limestone and protected Bower-Barff exterior iron. These data do not measure a 1904 RGB value or exact seventeen-year dirt map. Existing restrained finish variation remains; the new pattern adds no baked directional shadows. Modern references bound construction and material separation only. The family typescript remains a textual comparison only, with unresolved underlying rights unchanged; no new asset derives from it. These maps reuse the already committed original courtyard clay/mortar studies and numeric course schedule.

function.note: The house of John Jacob Glessner (1843-1936) and Frances Macbeth Glessner, designed by H. H. Richardson and built by Norcross Brothers, 1886-1887; the family lived here from December 1887 (Glessner 1923; HABS data p. 1). The west wing was the family's stable and carriage house (see range_west_wing).

built.note: The marker: 'John Glessner Residence. Built 1887'; the family moved in that December.
